analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and pays for them with new taxes on high earners and investment income.
analysis.headline: The bill would boost Social Security benefits for retirees, disabled workers, and widows, funded by removing the payroll tax cap and taxing large investment income; introduced with five Democratic senators, it has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since July 2026 with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise Social Security checks across the board, use an inflation index that better reflects what seniors buy, raise the minimum benefit for long-time low earners, add credits for years spent caring for children or disabled relatives, and cut the five-month wait for disability benefits. It would pay for this by applying the 12.4% Social Security tax to all wages with no cap, and by adding a 12.4% tax on investment income above $400,000 a year. It also directs the Social Security Administration to rebuild its customer-service workforce and keep field offices open.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 70 million Social Security beneficiaries and future retirees. Retirees get a benefit increase and a cost-of-living adjustment based on whichever inflation index is higher. Long-time low earners get a minimum benefit set at up to 125% of the poverty line. Beneficiaries with incomes under $35,000 ($50,000 for couples) stop paying federal income tax on their benefits. Caregivers get up to five years of credit toward benefits. Disabled applicants skip the five-month waiting period, and disabled beneficiaries who can work some keep benefits at a gradual reduction instead of losing them outright. Widows and widowers in two-earner households get higher survivor benefits, children get benefits through age 26 if in college, and grandchildren raised by relatives get easier access. The bill also rebuilds SSA's customer-service staff and keeps field offices open, which helps anyone who has to call or visit the agency.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors, disabled workers, widows, low earners

how_it_helps.text: Raises benefits across the board by moving the top benefit formula breakpoint from 90% to 93% of average wages, effective for 2027-2036.
Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to whichever is higher: the standard inflation index or the index for spending by people 62 and older, which better reflects seniors' medical costs.
Sets a new minimum benefit for long-term workers, rising with years worked up to 125% of the federal poverty guideline for those with 30 or more years of coverage.
Raises the income thresholds at which Social Security benefits become taxable to $35,000 for individuals and $50,000 for couples, ending income tax on benefits for many middle-income retirees.
Adds caregiver credits: up to five years counted as earnings at 50% of the national average wage for people who spent 960+ hours a year caring for young children or chronically dependent relatives.

Eliminates the five-month waiting period before disability benefits begin, and replaces the cliff where disabled beneficiaries lose all benefits when they work with a gradual reduction of $1 in benefits for each $2 earned above the substantial-work threshold.

Improves survivor benefits for widows and widowers from two-income households, extends children's benefits to half-time college students under 26, and makes it easier for children raised by grandparents or other relatives to qualify.

Pays for the increases by removing the annual cap on wages subject to the 12.4% Social Security tax and adding a 12.4% tax on net investment income above $400,000, with earnings above the old cap earning only a 1% benefit factor — protecting the trust fund by shifting the burden to the highest earners.

Directs SSA to rebuild its customer-service workforce, keep field offices open, protect beneficiary data, and resume mailing annual benefit statements — responses to service cutbacks that affect anyone who needs the agency's help.

analysis.who_pays: High earners and large investors. Every dollar of wages would become subject to the 12.4% Social Security tax — half paid by the worker, half by the employer — where today wages above the annual cap (about $184,000 in 2026) are exempt. Self-employed high earners pay the full 12.4% themselves. People with net investment income above $400,000 (plus the existing 3.8% levy above $200,000/$250,000) would pay 12.4% on that income, hitting capital gains, dividends, and pass-through earnings. Businesses that pay large salaries above the cap also bear the employer share. Above-cap earnings would earn only a 1% benefit factor, so most of those paying get little back.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, their employers, big investors

drawbacks.text: The tax changes are permanent while most benefit increases sunset after 2036 — the bill text requires benefits to be recomputed back to pre-increase levels for months after December 2036, so high earners would keep paying but the headline benefit raises would be temporary as written.

Removing the cap means the highest earners pay 12.4% on all wages while earning almost nothing back on those dollars (a 1% benefit factor), breaking the traditional link between what you pay in and what you get out — a fairness objection opponents raise even when the money goes to low-income beneficiaries.

Employers' share of the payroll tax on all wages above the cap is a new cost on high-salary businesses, which economists argue can ultimately show up as slower wage growth or hiring at the top of the pay scale.

A 12.4% levy on investment income above $400,000, stacked on the existing 3.8% net investment income tax, raises the total tax on large capital gains and dividends and could discourage some investment; it also adds administrative complexity for investors, estates, and trusts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary beneficiaries the gains are large and concrete: higher checks, a senior-weighted inflation adjustment, a poverty-floor minimum benefit, caregiver credits, and faster disability benefits, paid for by people at the very top of the income scale. The strongest honest objections are about design rather than direction: the tax increases are permanent while most benefit enhancements expire after 2036 as the bill is drafted, the repeal of the wage cap breaks the pay-in/pay-out link for the highest earners, and the new investment-income tax adds complexity and may slightly damp investment. On balance it is a large transfer from the top few percent of earners and investors to tens of millions of retirees, disabled workers, and survivors — though without a Congressional Budget Office or Social Security actuary score in the record, the exact solvency math cannot be verified from the provided sources.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late July 2026 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and with the session ending in early January 2027 it sits with little time left.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the Social Security 2100 Act on July 21, 2026, joined by Democratic Senators Slotkin, Luján, Whitehouse, and Duckworth.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the committee that handles Social Security legislation.
In the months since, the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action — the bill's entire recorded history is the referral.
No Republican has cosponsored the bill, so it has no visible path to the floor of a chamber where major legislation generally needs at least some bipartisan backing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners, their employers, and large investors are better off so far, because the bill's new taxes on wages above the cap and on investment income above $400,000 have not moved an inch. Beneficiaries gain nothing yet either — the bill is no closer to law than on the day it was introduced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and investors, so far

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security 2100 Act on July 21, 2026 and is championing the benefit increases funded by taxes on high earners.

for.name: Sens. Elissa Slotkin, Martin Heinrich 'Luján', Sheldon Whitehouse, and Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only four cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Mike Crapo)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 21, 2026 and has taken no recorded action since — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 96 non-Democratic senators has cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the bipartisan support typically needed to move major legislation.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and all four cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on; no vote has been taken, so the partisan shape is inferred from sponsorship, not roll calls.

industries.note: Would owe a new 12.4% tax on net investment income above $400,000 — capital gains, dividends, and pass-through earnings — on top of the existing 3.8% levy. This is the group whose money would fund most of the benefit increases, so its interest in stopping the bill runs directly against beneficiaries.

Wages above the annual cap (about $184,000 in 2026) would become subject to the 12.4% Social Security tax with almost nothing returned in benefits (a 1% factor), and self-employed high earners would pay the full 12.4% on all net earnings.
Employers would pay the matching 6.2% payroll tax on every dollar of wages above the current cap, a new cost for firms with many six- and seven-figure salaries.

industries.industry: Social Security Administration workforce and field offices
industries.note: The bill directs SSA to rebuild its customer-service staff and keep field offices open, reversing service cutbacks — the rare provision whose beneficiaries (the public needing service) and the institution (the agency) are aligned.

analysis.trajectory: With the 119th Congress ending January 3, 2027, no hearing or markup scheduled, and no Republican cosponsors, the bill is very unlikely to advance. Bills referred to Senate Finance this late in a two-year session with a single-digit sponsorship almost always die quietly when the Congress expires; reintroduction in the next Congress would be the realistic next step.
